newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria c.bank liquidity drain helps battered lev.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria c.bank liquidity drain helps battered lev.

text.p: Bulgaria's central bank decision to curb commercial banks' liquidity by raising minimum reserve requirements has started to relieve pressure on the battered lev, a Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) official said.

"This typical liquidity draining measure boosted the lev today and it is expected to dissuade banks from converting free levs into foreign currency," head of BNB's Lev Currency Operations department Georgi Petkov told Reuters.

Last night the BNB said it had decided to raise the total amount of banks' minimum reserves, requiring banks to place with the central bank each month 11 percent of the deposits they have attracted the month before, instead of 10 percent.
Some banks increased dollar sales today in a bid to boost their lev liquidity ahead of this month's payments of reserves for December, traders said.
This helped the lev rebound to 635-645 per dollar in the afternoon from 665-675 at the opening, commercial bank dealers said.

The lev traded at 507-510 per dollar on December 30, the last trading day of 1996 for the local market. It slumped to 720-750 on Monday amid political instability following Prime Minister Zhan Videnov's resignation in December.

Local commercial banks will have to place some 20 billion levs more with the central bank this month to meet the new minimum reserve requirements, bringing the total to some 105 billion levs according to first estimates, Petkov said.
However, a further rise in minimum reserve requirements could make banks with low lev and foreign exchange liquidity suffer serious problems, he added.

Under local banking regulations the upper limit of minimum required reserves is set at 15 percent of deposits which banks have attracted in levs and in foreign currency from companies and individuals.

Two cuts in as many weeks in the portion of the minimum reserves which banks can use on an average daily basis for emergency refinancing each month are also in the lev's favour, because they divert levs from the forex market, dealers said.

The BNB cut that portion to 30 percent from 40 percent of the total amount of reserves on January 3, just a week after a similar cut from 50 percent and ahead of large interest and maturity payments on government securities due this month. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
